claim.pdf_says: FUNCTION  FORMATTED-TIME  ( argument-1 argument-2 [ argument-3 ] )   -- with FUNCTION and FORMATTED-TIME both printed UNDERLINED (required words per 5.2.6.2)
claim.markdown_says: FUNCTION FORMATTED-TIME ( argument-1 argument-2 [ argument-3 ] )   -- no underline markup at all
claim.why_it_matters: Underlining is the standard's own notation for a REQUIRED word. The transcription applies it inconsistently: it IS preserved on page 895 (`<u>FUNCTION</u>  <u>HIGHEST-ALGEBRAIC</u>  ( argument-1 )`) and page 902 (`<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>INTEGER-PART</u> ( argument-1 )`), but dropped in the general formats on pages 892 (15.41.2), 894 (15.42.2), 897 (15.44.2), 898 (15.45.2), 899 (15.46.2), 900 (15.47.2) and 901 (15.48.2). On these particular pages every word in the format is required, so no legal syntax is made to look illegal and no optional word is made to look required -- the loss is presentational only. Recorded as a document-wide convention inconsistency, not a local semantic defect.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED as a page-892 content discrepancy. The claim's raw typographic observation is accurate, but it fails every test for a ledgerable finding.

WHAT I SEE IN THE PRINTED GLYPHS (spec_p892.png, 300dpi, section 15.41.2 at approx. y=773): the line reads `FUNCTION  FORMATTED-TIME  ( argument-1 argument-2 [ argument-3 ] )`. A continuous rule runs under `FUNCTION` and a second, separate rule runs under `FORMATTED-TIME`. Nothing from the opening parenthesis rightward is underlined. The two uppercase words are the ONLY uppercase words in the format, and BOTH are underlined. Markdown line 35704 of specs/ISO_COBOL.md is `FUNCTION FORMATTED-TIME ( argument-1 argument-2 [ argument-3 ] )` with no <u> markup. So the underline rendition does differ.

(1) NO CONTENT IS LOST -- THE DIFFERENCE IS PURELY TYPOGRAPHIC. Every token, word, parenthesis, bracket and metalanguage term is transcribed character-for-character correctly and in the correct order. Not one glyph of the format is missing, added, or reordered. The sole difference is the presence of a typographic rule. The rubric directs rejection when the difference is only formatting.

(2) THE UNDERLINE IS FULLY REDUNDANT IN THIS PARTICULAR FORMAT, SO NO DERIVABLE SYNTAX CHANGES. Underlining discriminates keywords (uppercase + underlined = required, per the transcribed 5.2.7/5.2.6 text at lines 2631 and 2644) from optional words (uppercase + NOT underlined). That contrast can only carry information when a format contains BOTH kinds. This format contains no optional words at all -- both uppercase words are underlined in print. Optionality here is carried entirely by the brackets around `argument-3`, and those brackets ARE transcribed. A reader deriving the syntax of FORMATTED-TIME from the markdown reaches exactly the same grammar as one reading the PDF. The claimant concedes this outright ("the loss is presentational only", "not a local semantic defect") -- i.e. the claim disavows being a page-892 content discrepancy in its own text.

(3) THE CLAIM MATERIALLY MISSTATES THE SCOPE, WHICH IS THE ONLY THING THAT MAKES IT LOOK LIKE A PAGE FINDING. It frames the drop as 7 named pages deviating from a preserved norm. I counted the actual distribution across chapter 15: only 22 of 75 intrinsic-function general formats carry <u> markup; 53 of 75 do not. The unmarked form is the DOMINANT behaviour, not a seven-page lapse. The markup is also applied incoherently WITHIN single formats -- line 34556 `<u>FUNCTION</u> CONVERT ( ... )` and line 38296 `<u>FUNCTION</u> TEST-NUMVAL ( ... )` underline FUNCTION but leave the function-name bare. That is the signature of a global transcription-pipeline artifact, not a defect localised to page 892. Ledgering it against page 892 (and 6 sibling pages) misattributes a document-wide rendering property to specific pages.

(4) THE TRANSCRIPTION ALREADY RECORDS UNDERLINE SEMANTICS BY A DIFFERENT, DELIBERATE MECHANISM. Throughout the document, required-word status is captured in prose annotations of the form "**Figure notes (...)** `X` and `Y` are underlined in the printed standard (required words)" -- see lines 3923, 3967, 4104, 4318, 4550, 4698, 4745, 4791, 4840, 4874, 6181-6219. Inline <u> is incidental markup, not the document's convention for conveying this information.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM'S REASONING, WHICH I NOTE BUT WHICH DOES NOT CHANGE THE VERDICT: the claim asserts "no optional word is made to look required". That half is true but it is the harmless direction. The direction that actually applies is the reverse -- per 5.2.6/5.2.7 an uppercase word without an underline denotes an OPTIONAL word, so stripping the rules renders two REQUIRED words as apparently optional. The claim analysed the wrong failure direction. This still does not make the finding real: FUNCTION and the intrinsic-function-name are self-evidently unomittable (dropping FORMATTED-TIME leaves no function to invoke), and since 53 of 75 formats in this chapter are equally unmarked, underline-absence carries no signal a reader could act on.

Verdict: a genuine typographic difference, but not a content discrepancy for page 892 -- formatting only, meaning-preserving, and misscoped. real=false.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a page-892 defect. Accurate as a raw observation (the PDF underlines both `FUNCTION` and `FORMATTED-TIME`; markdown line 35704 has no <u> markup) but not ledgerable: the token content is transcribed exactly and completely, the underline is redundant in this format because it contains no optional words for the required/optional contrast to distinguish (optionality is carried by the brackets around argument-3, which are preserved), and the derived syntax is identical from either source. The scope is also misstated -- <u> markup is present in only 22 of 75 chapter-15 intrinsic-function general formats and absent from 53, and is applied inconsistently even within single formats (line 34556 `<u>FUNCTION</u> CONVERT (...)`, line 38296 `<u>FUNCTION</u> TEST-NUMVAL (...)` underline FUNCTION but not the function-name), so this is a document-wide transcription-pipeline rendering property, not a defect on pages 892/894/897/898/899/900/901. Separately, the claim's harm analysis points the wrong way: absence of an underline denotes an OPTIONAL word per 5.2.6/5.2.7, so the effect is required words rendered as apparently optional, not optional words rendered as required. If this is to be tracked at all it belongs as a single global note about underline rendition in the transcription, not as a per-page figure defect.
